content:
A belated announcement of a paper with @Brian Nugent: Sorries Are Not the Hard Part.
Long story short, agents are very good at proofs, less good at making statements, and much worse at definitions.

Claude autoformalized the Grothendieck vanishing theorem (took 6 days with Claude), Brian heroically reviewed all 5k LOC Claude produced, as if it were a Mathlib PR. Then Claude iterated on Brian's review for another 2 weeks, and Brian heroically reviewed it again. AFAIK, this is the first time a large autoformalization project was carefully reviewed line-by-line.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13925

I think the paper may give slightly too much credit to the AI, as if the resulting definitions and API choices had emerged independently from the agent rather than being strongly shaped by the prompting process.

Reading the "human-prompts-gv.txt" file, it looks like the agents were strongly steered by the human prompts and by the surrounding workflow. The prompts repeatedly pushed the agents toward concrete local progress, smth like close sorries, keep going, pick a task from "plan.md", make every cycle produce progress, and make the project compile with default heartbeats.

In a real agent environment, prompting is necessarily adaptive. You start with an initial plan, then adjust the prompts in response to the Lean code the agent actually produces.

This matters because many of the issues later found by Brian seem consistent with that objective function. For example, Brian’s review repeatedly says that the code proves exactly what was needed locally instead of building the right general API. He asks for a major file-structure refactor, for less ad hoc API around topological Krull dimension, for sheaf cohomology API instead of repeatedly unfolding H into Ext, and for several statements to be generalized from the specific situation needed in the proof to the natural reusable theorem.

A few concrete examples make this clear.

First, the repeated prompts about compiling with default heartbeats suggest that the agents were trying to solve performance problems by local optimization or by heartbeat overrides, and you had to keep pushing them back toward normal Lean compilation standards.

Second, the recurring "prove sorries directly" style of prompting rewards local proof closure. That naturally encourages decomposing a hard goal into whatever intermediate lemmas make the current proof pass, even if those lemmas are not the right public API.

Third, Brian’s review repeatedly identifies exactly this pattern, results stated for overly specific sheaf objects instead of the more general presheaf-plus-sheaf-condition formulation; results stated for an injective presentation when they should be stated for an arbitrary short exact complex; and vanishing implications where the more natural theorem should be an isomorphism.

Fourth, the review says that the code often unfolds the definition of sheaf cohomology H in terms of Ext instead of building a dedicated API for H. That is a classic sign of a proof-driven development process, smth like open the definition, solve the immediate goal, and move on. It is not the same thing as designing a stable abstraction layer.

Brian’s main criticism is about definitions and API design, and that seems closely connected, IMO, to the process. The agents were repeatedly pushed to make progress, close sorries, and compile, rather than to design the cleanest reusable definitions first.
